teaching_brief.unit_overview: A wider world depth study on the causes, course and ending of the First World War. Students need a tight grasp of long-term tensions (alliances, Anglo-German rivalry, Slav nationalism), the trigger and escalation of July 1914, why stalemate set in on the Western Front, the wider war (Gallipoli, Jutland, U-boats, convoys), and the combination of factors that broke Germany in 1918. The four question types (4-mark source analysis, 12-mark source utility, 8-mark narrative account, 16-mark source-based essay) reward source skills plus deep contextual knowledge — every lesson should arm students with both specific detail (dates, names, numbers) and the analytical framework to weigh causes, consequences and significance.

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students treat the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand as 'the cause' of WWI, when it was the trigger that activated longer-term tensions (alliances, Weltpolitik, naval race, Balkan nationalism) which had been building for decades.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: AQA principal examiner reports on GCSE History 8145 Paper 1 Section B Option BA

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students describe the plan as a 'bad plan that always would fail', missing that its rigid timetable, Russian mobilisation speed, Belgian resistance and the Battle of the Marne all combined to cause its collapse.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: AQA examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students depict the Western Front as four years of static, identical, futile slaughter — missing the evolution of tactics (creeping barrage, combined arms, tanks, stormtroopers) that broke the deadlock by 1918.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: Gary Sheffield, Forgotten Victory and revisionist scholarship summarised in History Today

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: The 'lions led by donkeys' / Blackadder view dominates student writing — generals are dismissed as incompetent butchers without weighing the learning curve and operational successes of 1918.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: Gary Sheffield, History Today; AQA examiner reports flagging caricatured generalisations

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students treat Gallipoli as solely a British failure, missing the ANZAC, French and Indian contribution, the strategic logic of knocking Turkey out of the war, and the specific operational reasons for failure.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: Imperial War Museums and AQA examiner commentary on the wider war

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students claim the USA joined the war 'because of the Lusitania' (sunk May 1915) — the actual entry was April 1917, triggered by unrestricted submarine warfare from Feb 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: AQA mark scheme indicative content for narrative-account questions on US entry

common_misconceptions_unit_level.misconception: Students give a single-cause answer (usually 'America joined' or 'the blockade') instead of weighing US manpower, the Hundred Days, the failure of the Spring Offensive, the blockade, internal collapse and the role of Foch and Haig together.
common_misconceptions_unit_level.source: AQA examiner reports on 16-mark source-based essays for Option BA

examiner_signals_unit_level.signal: Top-band 8-mark narrative accounts on this option weave a clear causal chain through three or four linked events with explicit connectives ('this led to...', 'as a consequence...') rather than chronological lists.
examiner_signals_unit_level.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.1 and principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

examiner_signals_unit_level.signal: 12-mark source utility responses on this option must integrate content + provenance + own contextual knowledge for both sources — examiners flag answers that only weigh provenance ('this is biased so not useful') as capping at the lower bands.
examiner_signals_unit_level.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 Section B source-utility questions

examiner_signals_unit_level.signal: 16-mark source-based essays reward a sustained judgement on the named factor versus alternative factors — strong responses use the source as a springboard and bring in contextual evidence from across the wider period.
examiner_signals_unit_level.source: AQA mark scheme indicative content for 16-mark questions on Option BA

examiner_signals_unit_level.signal: Specific named detail (e.g. 'BEF of 100,000 men in August 1914', 'Haber process for nitrates from 1914', 'Zimmermann Telegram intercepted Jan 1917') consistently distinguishes top-band responses from generic accounts.
examiner_signals_unit_level.source: AQA examiner commentary on indicative content for high-band responses

historiography_notes.framing: Fritz Fischer's thesis on German war aims (Griff nach der Weltmacht, 1961) versus Christopher Clark's Sleepwalkers (2012) which spreads responsibility across the European powers — useful for framing Anglo-German rivalry and the July Crisis without overloading GCSE students.
historiography_notes.use: Background only — surface as a sentence-level note in causes lessons, not as required examinable content.

historiography_notes.framing: Alan Clark's The Donkeys (1961) and the Blackadder caricature versus revisionist work by Gary Sheffield, Peter Simkins and Dan Todman emphasising the BEF's learning curve and operational successes in 1918.
historiography_notes.use: Surface in trench-warfare and Hundred Days lessons to inoculate students against the donkeys cliche.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Kaiser Wilhelm II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: German emperor whose Weltpolitik, dismissal of Bismarck and naval-race brinkmanship destabilised European diplomacy.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne whose assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 triggered the July Crisis.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Gavrilo Princip
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Bosnian Serb nationalist (Black Hand-linked) whose shots in Sarajevo opened the path to war.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tsar Nicholas II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Russian emperor whose mobilisation order on 30 July 1914 escalated the crisis; Russian withdrawal in 1917 reshaped German strategy.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alfred von Schlieffen
key_individuals_and_groups.role: German Chief of Staff who designed the war plan to defeat France in six weeks via Belgium before turning east.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Helmuth von Moltke (the Younger)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: German Chief of Staff in 1914 who modified and executed the Schlieffen Plan and was sacked after the Marne.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: General Joseph Joffre
key_individuals_and_groups.role: French commander whose counter-attack on the Marne in September 1914 saved Paris and ended the Schlieffen timetable.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig
key_individuals_and_groups.role: British commander on the Western Front from December 1915 — Somme, Passchendaele, the Hundred Days.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Marshal Ferdinand Foch
key_individuals_and_groups.role: French general appointed Allied Generalissimo in April 1918 who coordinated the war-winning counter-offensive.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: General Erich Ludendorff
key_individuals_and_groups.role: German Quartermaster General and de facto commander; architect of the 1918 Spring Offensive.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Paul von Hindenburg
key_individuals_and_groups.role: German Chief of the General Staff; political-military partner of Ludendorff in the silent dictatorship of 1916-18.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Admiral John Jellicoe
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Commander of the British Grand Fleet at Jutland (May 1916).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Admiral Reinhard Scheer
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Commander of the German High Seas Fleet at Jutland.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Winston Churchill
key_individuals_and_groups.role: First Lord of the Admiralty whose advocacy for the Dardanelles led to Gallipoli; resigned after the failure.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: President Woodrow Wilson
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US president who kept America neutral until April 1917 and shaped the armistice via the Fourteen Points.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Vladimir Lenin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Bolshevik leader whose seizure of power in October 1917 led to Brest-Litovsk and Russia's exit from the war.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The BEF (British Expeditionary Force)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Britain's small professional army of 1914 that grew via Kitchener volunteers, conscription (1916) and the Pals battalions.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The ANZAC forces
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Australian and New Zealand troops central to the Gallipoli campaign and the Western Front (Pozieres, Hamel).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Black Hand
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Serbian nationalist secret society linked to Princip and the Sarajevo plot.

lessons.title: Europe in 1894: Empires, Alliances and the Long Fuse
lessons.description: Setting the scene — the five Great Powers, Bismarck's system unravelling and Europe's drift into two blocs.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Alliance System opener; context for Triple Alliance and Franco-Russian Alliance
learning_outcomes: Identify the five European Great Powers in 1894 and their core interests.
Explain how Bismarck's diplomatic system aimed to isolate France.
Describe how the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 ended that isolation.

lessons.title: The Alliance System and Splendid Isolation
lessons.description: The Triple Alliance, the Entente Cordiale (1904) and the Triple Entente (1907) lock Europe into two camps.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Alliance System; Britain abandoning Splendid Isolation; relations between Entente powers
learning_outcomes: Explain the terms and motives of the Triple Alliance (1882) and Triple Entente (1907).
Analyse why Britain ended Splendid Isolation after 1900.
Evaluate how alliances raised the risk of a continental war becoming general.

lessons.title: Anglo-German Rivalry: Weltpolitik and the Naval Race
lessons.description: Wilhelm II's world policy, colonial friction and Tirpitz's dreadnought-for-dreadnought naval race with Britain.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Anglo-German rivalry; Kaiser's foreign policy aims; Weltpolitik; colonial tensions; European rearmament; Anglo-German naval race
learning_outcomes: Describe Weltpolitik and how it broke with Bismarck's continental focus.
Explain how the dreadnought race poisoned Anglo-German relations from 1906.
Evaluate the role of personality (Wilhelm II) versus structural rivalry.

lessons.title: Crisis Points: Morocco 1905 and 1911, Bosnia 1908-09
lessons.description: Three pre-war crises that hardened the alliance blocs and rehearsed brinkmanship.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Crises in Morocco (1905, 1911) and the Balkans (1908-09) and their effects on international relations
learning_outcomes: Describe the events of the Tangier (1905) and Agadir (1911) Moroccan crises.
Explain how the Bosnian Annexation Crisis humiliated Russia and angered Serbia.
Analyse how each crisis tightened alliance commitments and military planning.

lessons.title: Sarajevo and the July Crisis
lessons.description: Princip's bullets, the blank cheque, the ultimatum and the cascade of mobilisations that brought war.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Slav nationalism; Serbia and Austria-Hungary; assassination of Franz Ferdinand; the July Crisis
learning_outcomes: Sequence the events of 28 June to 4 August 1914 with accurate dates.
Explain the role of Slav nationalism, the Black Hand and the Austrian ultimatum.
Evaluate why diplomacy failed and war became general by early August.

lessons.title: The Schlieffen Plan and the Battle of the Marne
lessons.description: Germany's plan to knock France out in six weeks — and the BEF, Belgium and Joffre's counter-attack that wrecked it.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 / Part 2 — Schlieffen Plan and Belgium; reasons for outbreak; Schlieffen Plan failure and Battle of the Marne; contribution to stalemate
learning_outcomes: Describe the design and assumptions of the Schlieffen Plan.
Explain why Belgian resistance, BEF intervention and the Marne defeated it.
Analyse how the failure of the plan produced the stalemate of trench warfare.

lessons.title: Trench Warfare on the Western Front
lessons.description: How attack collapsed against defence — trenches, machine guns, artillery and the war of attrition.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — Western Front; military tactics and technology; trench warfare; war of attrition
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure of a trench system and a soldier's typical routine.
Explain how technology (machine guns, barbed wire, artillery, gas) favoured defence.
Evaluate the human and strategic costs of attritional warfare.

lessons.title: Verdun and the Somme, 1916
lessons.description: Falkenhayn's attempt to bleed France white and the British army's costly Somme offensive — the year of attrition.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — Key battles: Verdun, the Somme; reasons for, events and significance
learning_outcomes: Describe the strategic aims and key events of Verdun (Feb-Dec 1916) and the Somme (July-Nov 1916).
Explain why first-day Somme casualties were so heavy and what was learnt.
Evaluate the significance of 1916 for Britain, France and Germany.

lessons.title: Passchendaele and the Tactical Learning Curve
lessons.description: Third Ypres, the mud of 1917 and how the BEF was actually adapting — creeping barrage, tanks, combined arms.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — Passchendaele; reasons for, events and significance; military tactics and technology
learning_outcomes: Describe the events and conditions of Passchendaele (Third Ypres, July-Nov 1917).
Explain how British tactics evolved from 1915 to 1917 (creeping barrage, tanks, sound-ranging).
Evaluate the 'lions led by donkeys' verdict against revisionist evidence.

lessons.title: The Wider War: Gallipoli and Other Fronts
lessons.description: Trying to break the deadlock somewhere else — the Dardanelles gamble, ANZAC at Anzac Cove and the Eastern Front.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — War on other fronts; Gallipoli and its failure
learning_outcomes: Describe the strategic reasoning for the Dardanelles/Gallipoli campaign (1915).
Explain the operational reasons it failed and the cost to ANZAC and British forces.
Outline the war on the Eastern Front and the Italian Front in summary.

lessons.title: The War at Sea: Jutland, U-boats and Convoys
lessons.description: Jellicoe versus Scheer at Jutland, the U-boat threat to Britain's lifeline and the convoy system that beat it.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — War at sea; Jutland; U-Boat campaign and convoys
learning_outcomes: Describe the Battle of Jutland (May 1916) and debate over who 'won'.
Explain the German switch to unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917.
Analyse why the convoy system from May 1917 turned the U-boat war.

lessons.title: Russia Out, America In: 1917
lessons.description: Bolshevik revolution and Brest-Litovsk free German troops east; Zimmermann and the U-boats bring the USA into the war.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — Consequences of the Bolshevik Revolution and Russian withdrawal on German strategy; reasons for and impact of US entry
learning_outcomes: Explain why Russia withdrew from the war and what Brest-Litovsk gave Germany.
Describe the chain of events (Lusitania 1915, unrestricted submarine warfare 1917, Zimmermann Telegram) leading to US entry in April 1917.
Analyse the strategic impact on both Germany and the Allies of the 1917 turning point.

lessons.title: Spring Offensive, Hundred Days and Armistice
lessons.description: Ludendorff's last gamble, Foch and Haig's war-winning counter-attack, the blockade, the Kaiser's abdication and 11 November.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — Military developments in 1918; tactics and technology; Ludendorff Spring Offensive; Hundred Days; blockade; abdication; armistice; contribution of Haig and Foch
learning_outcomes: Describe the German Spring Offensive (March-July 1918) and why it ran out of steam.
Explain how the Hundred Days (Aug-Nov 1918) combined US manpower, tanks, air power and combined-arms tactics.
Evaluate the relative weight of the blockade, US entry, Allied generals (Haig and Foch) and German internal collapse in producing the armistice.

gaps.topic: Alan Clark's The Donkeys / Blackadder framing of generalship
gaps.issue: Spec does not require historiography but the donkeys cliche dominates student writing on this option. Resolved by surfacing revisionist work (Sheffield, Todman) inside Lessons 7 and 9 as a misconception inoculation rather than examinable content.

gaps.topic: Christopher Clark / Fritz Fischer historiographical debate on origins
gaps.issue: Background only. Surfaced as a one-sentence note in Lessons 1-5 to give students a sense of the debate without making it examinable.

gaps.topic: The Home Front (rationing, propaganda, women's war work)
gaps.issue: Not in this option's spec — sits in Britain Health/People and other thematic studies. Mentioning briefly only where it directly bears on the blockade in Lesson 13.
